title: 10 Easy Ways to Lower Your Energy Bill Before Summer
seo_title: 10 Ways to Lower Your Energy Bill
seo_description: Want lower AC bills this summer? Learn simple ways to reduce wasted energy, improve cooling efficiency, and know when to schedule HVAC service.
html:
If last summer’s cooling bills made you wince, spring is the time to do something about it. Once heat and humidity settle into Johnson City and the Tri-Cities, your air conditioner has to work harder every day to keep your home comfortable. If your system is dirty, outdated, poorly maintained, or fighting against air leaks and direct sunlight, that extra workload can show up quickly on your utility bill.

The good news is that you do not have to choose between comfort and savings. A few smart steps before peak cooling season can help improve efficiency, reduce strain on your AC, and lower your energy bill before summer is in full swing. Some changes are simple homeowner habits, while others are best handled by an HVAC professional who can spot performance issues early.

Here are 10 practical ways to get your home and cooling system ready before the Tri-Cities summer heat arrives.

Quick Answer: How Can You Lower Your Energy Bill Before Summer?

To lower your energy bill before summer, focus on three areas: simple home habits, energy-saving improvements, and HVAC system performance.

Start by changing your air filter, adjusting thermostat settings, using ceiling fans correctly, and blocking direct sunlight. Then look for air leaks, blocked vents, and ductwork problems that may be wasting cooled air. Finally, schedule AC maintenance before peak season so a technician can clean, inspect, and test your system before it is running every day.

For Tri-Cities homeowners, this matters because summer humidity can make an inefficient or poorly maintained AC work harder than it should.

1. Replace or Clean Your Air Filter

A dirty air filter makes your AC work harder to pull air through the system. That restricted airflow can increase energy use, reduce comfort, and put added strain on the blower motor and other components.

Check your filter before summer begins and replace or clean it if it looks dirty. Many homes need a filter change every one to three months, but homes with pets, allergies, heavy system use, or more dust may need changes more often.

This is one of the simplest and lowest-cost ways to help your cooling system breathe better.

2. Schedule an AC Tune-Up Before the Rush

An AC system can look fine from the outside and still have hidden issues that affect efficiency. Dirty coils, weak airflow, worn electrical components, low refrigerant, or drainage problems can all make your system work harder than necessary.

During a professional tune-up, a technician can inspect key components, test performance, check airflow, clean parts as needed, and catch early signs of wear. Scheduling maintenance before peak summer gives you time to address small issues before your AC is running daily.

For homeowners in Johnson City, Kingsport, Bristol, and nearby Tri-Cities communities, spring service is one of the smartest ways to prepare for a more reliable summer.

3. Adjust Your Thermostat Settings

Your thermostat has a direct impact on cooling costs. Setting it slightly higher when you are away or asleep can reduce how often your AC runs.

You do not have to make your home uncomfortable. Even small adjustments can help. Try raising the temperature a few degrees when the house is empty, then lowering it only when you need comfort.

Also, avoid setting the thermostat much lower than your desired temperature. Most central AC systems do not cool faster just because the setting is lower. They simply run longer, which can waste energy.

4. Consider a Smart Thermostat

A smart thermostat can help reduce wasted cooling by adjusting temperatures based on your schedule, habits, or whether someone is home. This is especially helpful if your family’s routine changes throughout the week.

A smart thermostat may also help you notice patterns, such as when your home takes too long to cool down or when the system runs more than expected. That information can be useful if you are trying to decide whether your AC needs maintenance, repair, or replacement.

Before buying one, make sure the thermostat is compatible with your HVAC system. Some heat pumps, multi-stage systems, and high-efficiency equipment may need specific controls.

5. Seal Air Leaks Around the Home

If cooled air is escaping through gaps around windows, doors, attic access points, or utility openings, your AC has to work harder to replace it.

Before summer, walk through your home and look for drafts or visible gaps. Weatherstripping, caulk, and insulation improvements can help reduce wasted cooling. This is especially helpful in older homes throughout Northeast Tennessee where small leaks around doors, windows, crawl spaces, and attic areas can add up.

Less wasted air means your AC can spend more time maintaining comfort and less time fighting the house itself.

6. Use Ceiling Fans the Right Way

Ceiling fans do not lower the temperature of a room, but they help people feel cooler by moving air across the skin. That means you may be able to keep the thermostat slightly higher without feeling uncomfortable.

In summer, ceiling fans should typically rotate counterclockwise to push air downward. Turn fans off when you leave the room, since fans cool people, not empty spaces.

This small habit can make a room feel more comfortable without asking your AC to do all the work.

7. Block Heat From the Sun

Sunlight streaming through windows can heat up your home quickly, especially during the afternoon. Closing blinds, curtains, or shades during the hottest parts of the day can reduce heat gain and help your AC keep up.

This can make a noticeable difference in rooms that face west or get strong afternoon sun. For better results, consider light-colored window coverings, blackout curtains, or exterior shading where practical.

The less heat your home absorbs during the day, the less cooling your AC has to produce later.

8. Check Vents and Registers

Blocked vents can cause uneven cooling and make your system work harder than necessary. Walk through your home and make sure furniture, rugs, curtains, or storage items are not blocking supply or return vents.

Also, avoid closing too many vents in unused rooms. Many central HVAC systems are designed to move a specific amount of air. Closing vents can increase pressure in the ductwork, reduce efficiency, and cause comfort problems in other rooms.

If certain rooms in your home are always warmer than others, the issue may be airflow, not just thermostat settings.

9. Look for Ductwork Problems

Leaky, damaged, or poorly insulated ductwork can waste cooled air before it ever reaches your living spaces. This is especially common in older homes, homes with ductwork in attics or crawl spaces, and homes with rooms that never seem to cool evenly.

Signs of duct problems include weak airflow, dusty air, hot and cold spots, or an AC that runs constantly. If you notice these issues, an HVAC technician can inspect the ductwork and recommend sealing, repairs, insulation, or airflow improvements.

Fixing duct problems can help your system deliver cooling where you actually need it instead of losing conditioned air along the way.

10. Know When Your AC Is the Problem

Sometimes, high energy bills are not caused by habits, sunlight, or small home issues. They are caused by an aging or struggling air conditioner.
If you have already changed the filter, adjusted the thermostat, blocked sunlight, and checked vents but your system still runs constantly, the issue may be the AC itself.

An older AC may use more energy to produce less comfort, especially if it is more than 10 to 15 years old, needs frequent repairs, short cycles, makes unusual noises, or cannot control humidity well. In that case, maintenance or repair may help, but replacement may be the better long-term solution.

The goal is not to replace equipment too early. The goal is to understand whether your current system is still worth investing in.

FAQs About Lowering Your Energy Bill Before Summer

Does turning the thermostat way down cool the house faster?

No. Most central AC systems cool at the same rate regardless of how low you set the thermostat. Setting it much lower usually makes the system run longer, which can waste energy and increase your bill.

How often should I schedule AC maintenance?

Most homeowners should schedule AC maintenance once a year, ideally in spring before peak cooling season. Regular maintenance helps improve reliability, supports efficiency, and gives a technician a chance to catch small issues early.

Can a dirty air filter really raise my energy bill?

Yes. A dirty filter restricts airflow, which makes your AC work harder to cool your home. It can also contribute to frozen coils, uneven cooling, longer run times, and added system strain.

Is it better to repair or replace an inefficient AC?

It depends on the age, condition, repair cost, and performance of the system. Repair may make sense for a newer unit with a minor issue. Replacement may be better if the system is older, inefficient, unreliable, or causing repeated comfort problems.

Do smart thermostats work for every home?

Not always. Smart thermostats can be helpful, but compatibility matters. Before installing one, confirm that it works with your HVAC system, especially if you have a heat pump, multi-stage equipment, or high-efficiency cooling system.

Final Thoughts

Lowering your energy bill before summer does not have to mean giving up comfort. In many homes, simple steps like replacing filters, adjusting thermostat habits, sealing leaks, blocking sunlight, checking vents, and scheduling maintenance can help reduce wasted energy before the hottest weather arrives.
